``` ::: ::: ## Dropping Missing Values Use `dropna()` to remove rows with missing values in the columns required for analysis. ::: {#6f30167f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # drop rows where 'text' or 'retweet_count' is missing (value is NA or NaN) df_clean = df.dropna(subset=["text", "retweet_count"]) ``` ::: **Dropping Missing Values:** - Use `df.dropna()` to remove rows containing missing values (NA or NaN). - By default, it removes any row with at least one missing value. - Specify `subset` as a list of column names to only consider missing values in those columns for removal. - Use parentheses `()` or square brackets `[]` for the subset list. > **Note:** For data preprocessing, selectively drop rows with missing values only in columns relevant to your analysis to maintain data accuracy. ::: {#3e6aaeb6 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.shape # view original shape (num of rows, num of cols) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (430, 14) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#1aa9b8b5 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_clean.shape # shape after dropping rows with missing values ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (429, 14) ``` ::: ::: ## Filling Missing Values Use `fillna()` when a missing value should be replaced rather than removed. ::: {#9bcbb4d5 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # fill missing values in 'mentions' with a placeholder string df["mentions"] = df["mentions"].fillna("No Mentioned User") # view replaced values in 'mentions' column df.head(3)["mentions"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 0 No Mentioned User 1 @lizzie_hubbard2 @JetsettersFlyin @suziday123 ... 2 @craftbeerncl! @RidgesideBrewer @Manjitskitche... Name: mentions, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: **Filling Missing Values:** - Use `df.fillna(value)` to replace missing values in a specific column with a placeholder, such as a string. - Assign the result back to the column to update the DataFrame. ## Replacing Specific Values Use `replace()` to convert placeholder values into a more useful representation. ::: {#7637c41d .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # replace the placeholder string with 0 df["mentions"] = df["mentions"].replace("No Mentioned User", 0) # view replaced values in 'mentions' column df.head(3)["mentions"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0 0 1 @lizzie_hubbard2 @JetsettersFlyin @suziday123 ... 2 @craftbeerncl! @RidgesideBrewer @Manjitskitche... Name: mentions, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: **Replacing Specific Values:** - Use `df.replace(old_value, new_value)` to substitute specific values in a column. - This is useful for converting placeholders into more appropriate representations, like numbers. # Renaming and Creating Columns ## Renaming Columns Use `rename()` to make column names shorter and more descriptive. ::: {#77c508fe .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # rename 'text' to 'content' and 'created_at' to 'date' df = df.rename(columns={"text": "content", "created_at": "date"}) # view renamed columns df.head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: **Creating New Columns:** - First, clean the data by dropping rows with missing values in relevant columns using `df.dropna(subset=['column'])`. ### Applying Basic Column Operations Create a new column by applying a vectorized calculation to an existing column. ::: {#86a7847d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # create a new column 'followers_k' by dividing 'user.followers_count' by 1000 df["followers_k"] = df["user.followers_count"] / 1000 # view the new column alongside the original follower count df.head(3)[["followers_k", "user.followers_count"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: **Creating New Columns:** - Create new columns by performing vectorized operations on existing columns, e.g., `df['new_col'] = df['existing_col'] / 1000`. ### Applying a Custom Function Define a reusable function when the transformation is clearer as named logic. ::: {#dc848f7f .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} # define a function to calculate engagement rate (ER) as a percentage def calc_er(engagement_count, follower_count): return (engagement_count / follower_count) * 100 ``` ::: ::: {#964ca5a4 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # apply and assign the calculated engagement rate to a new column 'er_rt_fo' df["er_rt_fo"] = calc_er( df["retweet_count"], df["user.followers_count"], ) # view the new engagement rate column alongside the original metrics df.head(3)[["er_rt_fo", "retweet_count", "user.followers_count"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {#25e721a4 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # visualize the relationship between engagement rate & two other metrics ax = df[["er_rt_fo", "retweet_count", "user.followers_count"]].plot( subplots=True, title="Engagement Rate vs Retweets and Followers", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=592 height=459} ::: ::: **Creating New Columns:** - Define a function for complex calculations, such as efficiency ratio: ER = (effective cost / full cost) * 100. - Apply the function to DataFrame columns to generate new metrics. - Use `.values` if needed to extract array from Series. - Visualize relationships using `df.plot()` with `subplots=True` for separate plots, `figsize` for dimensions, and `kind` for plot types (default 'line', options include 'bar', 'hist', 'scatter', 'pie'). # Finding Duplicates Remove fully duplicated rows with `duplicated()`. ::: {#8d75cb82 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # drop fully duplicated rows (keep the first occurrence) # ~ is the negation operator df = df[~df.duplicated()] ``` ::: **Finding Duplicates:** - Use `df.duplicated()` to identify duplicate rows; it returns a boolean Series. - Use `~df.duplicated()` to keep only unique rows. - Specify `subset` as a list of columns to check for duplicates based on those columns only. - Use `keep=False` to mark all duplicates. Find users who posted multiple times on the same date by specifying a subset of columns. ::: {#d089d055 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # find duplicated rows based on 'user' and 'date' columns (keep all occurrences) df[df.duplicated(subset=["user", "date"], keep=False)].head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: # Grouping and Aggregation Use `groupby()` with `agg()` to compute summary statistics by group. The example below calculates total retweets and average follower count for each user. ::: {#de53748a .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} # group by 'user', then aggregate 'retweet_count' with sum # and 'user.followers_count' with mean df_agg = df.groupby("user").agg( {"retweet_count": "sum", "user.followers_count": "mean",} ) # view the aggregated result df_agg.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

You can compare the grouped result with the number of unique users: ::: {#bb4038b2 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # count unique users by dropping duplicates based on 'user' column df[~df.duplicated(subset="user")].shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` (390, 16) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#3e32fe61 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} # or simply count the number of unique users with nunique() df["user"].nunique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` 390 ``` ::: ::: # Melting and Pivoting ## Melting Data **Melting: wide → long** Use `melt()` to convert wide data into long format for analysis and plotting. ::: {#6d731497 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # create a sample wide-format DataFrame with pet types and counts df_wide = pd.DataFrame( data=[ ["cat", 4, 5], ["dog", 7, 4], ["rabbit", 2, 3], ], columns=["pet", "male", "female"], ) df_wide # view it ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}
pet male female
0 cat 4 5
1 dog 7 4
2 rabbit 2 3
``` ::: ::: Without arguments, `melt()` collapses all columns into variable-value pairs. ::: {#6d71f73c .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_wide.melt() # melt all cols into variable-value pairs (pivot longer) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}
variable value
0 pet cat
1 pet dog
2 pet rabbit
3 male 4
4 male 7
5 male 2
6 female 5
7 female 4
8 female 3
``` ::: ::: Specify identifier and value columns for a structured long-format result. ::: {#ef8c3634 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} melted_df = pd.melt( df_wide, id_vars=["pet"], # keep 'pet' as identifier column value_vars=["male", "female"], # value columns var_name="sex", # name for the new variable column value_name="count", # name for the new value column ) ``` ::: ## Pivoting Data **Pivot: long → wide** Pivot the long data back to wide format: ::: {#166b4df1 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_pivot = melted_df.pivot( index="pet", # identifier column becomes index columns="sex", # categories in variable column becomes new columns values="count", # value column becomes new values ).reset_index() # reset index to turn 'pet' back into a column df_pivot.columns.name = None # remove the name of the columns index df_pivot # view the pivoted DataFrame ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
pet female male
0 cat 5 4
1 dog 4 7
2 rabbit 3 2
``` ::: ::: Use `pivot_table()` instead of `pivot()` when there are duplicate index/column combinations, and specify an aggregation function like `aggfunc='mean'` to summarize duplicates. For example, if we have duplicate pet entries: ::: {#f1aef3f1 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} # create a sample DataFrame with duplicate pet entries df_long = pd.DataFrame( data=[ ["cat", "male", 4], ["cat", "female", 5], ["dog", "female", 7], ["dog", "male", 4], ["rabbit", "male", 2], ["rabbit", "female", 3], ], columns=["pet", "sex", "count"], ) df_long # view the long-format DataFrame with duplicates ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}

2 dog female 7
3 dog male 4
4 rabbit male 2
5 rabbit female 3
